summary: This document summarizes a workshop on Smart Object Security held in Paris on 23 March 2012. Participants shared thoughts on using existing and widely deployed security mechanisms for smart objects, and the report lists conclusions and recommendations for the IETF.

plainLanguage.summary: Tiny connected devices, often called smart objects, need to be secure but have very little memory, power and bandwidth. RFC 7397 reports on a 2012 workshop where experts compared their experience and concluded that existing security protocols can be made to work if they are chosen and combined carefully.

subtitle: What a 2012 workshop concluded about reusing existing security protocols on tiny, constrained smart objects.

tldr.problem: Smart objects are too constrained for security to be added casually, yet they need protection, and the many deployment scenarios and business models make a single security architecture unrealistic.
tldr.mechanism: A one-day workshop in Paris gathered position papers and invited talks on requirements, implementation experience, authorization and credential provisioning, and discussed how existing IETF security protocols can be customized for constrained devices.
tldr.outcome: Participants concluded that IETF security protocols such as TLS and DTLS are implementable on constrained devices, that new cryptographic algorithms are not the answer, and that integration and follow-up work matter more than a universal design.

today: RFC 7397 is an Informational report from December 2014 on a workshop held in Paris on March 23, 2012. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The report itself notes that follow-up work led to the IETF's Light-Weight Implementation Guidance, DTLS In Constrained Environments, and Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments efforts.

sections.title: Why the Workshop Happened
sections.content:
In early 2011 the Internet Architecture Board solicited position statements for a workshop on interconnecting smart objects with the Internet, to gather the wider community's experience with running IETF protocols in constrained environments. That workshop was held in Prague on March 25, 2011, and RFC 6574 summarizes it and suggests next steps. In the months that followed, new efforts began, including the Light-Weight Implementation Guidance working group and hackathons at IETF 80 and IETF 81.

Security contributions from the Constrained RESTful Environments and Transport Layer Security working groups made it clear that more discussion was needed, and that it had to include implementation and deployment experience as well as a shared view of how the pieces fit into a larger architecture. The Smart Object Security workshop was organized to bring together separate security discussions that were happening in different working groups and industry fora. It was a one-day workshop held before IETF 83 in Paris on March 23, 2012.

The organizers sought input on what credential-issuing techniques had been deployed, what extensions make existing security protocols fit smart objects better, what kinds of credentials are common, what experience had been gained with application-, transport-, network- and link-layer security, how clever implementations make protocols fit, and what lessons existing deployments hold. This RFC reports on those discussions and lists the participants' recommendations; its views are those of the participants, not necessarily of the authors or the IAB. It is a report on proceedings, not a specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Earlier work on connecting small devices raised many open questions about security, so experts met for a day in Paris in 2012 to compare notes. This document is the record of what they discussed and recommended, not a new standard.

sections.title: Requirements and Use Cases
sections.content:
Designing security for smart objects starts from the communication relationships, the constraints and the threats. A single protocol's security considerations section is not enough: a useful solution requires analysing the larger ecosystem. The RFC lists the questions that arise: who the actors are, who provisions credentials, what constraints the design faces, what type of authorization each actor needs, and what tasks the customer deploying the solution is expected to perform.

The answers vary widely. A smart meter is one of the more complex deployments because of the energy sector's history, whereas a small smart lighting system is cheap and meant to be set up as easily as its dumb predecessor. In the consumer market, security should not add overhead to installation, because a user who has to spend more time or effort will likely skip it. Devices are often retrofitted into existing infrastructure and bought and installed by consumers, so they come partly preinstalled and tend to interoperate only with the vendor's own servers.

The RFC warns about defaults and longevity. It is still common to ship devices with default passwords, and a device should not sit in a vulnerable but Internet-connected state before the consumer has configured it. Devices that need human interaction to update their software will likely be a problem, especially when service schedules run from five to twenty-five years, and threats seen as pranks have a habit of evolving into destructive attacks. The RFC also notes that vulnerabilities matter at large scale, for example in smart meters and the power grid.
sections.plainLanguage: A light bulb and a power meter need different protection, so the design has to start from who uses the device and what it does. Security must be easy enough that people do not skip it, and devices must be able to receive fixes for many years.

sections.title: Implementation Experience
sections.content:
Three invited talks covered a tiny implementation of the Constrained Application Protocol protected by Datagram Transport Layer Security, a TLS implementation using raw public keys, and general experience implementing public key cryptography on smart object devices. All three showed that implementing IETF security protocols on constrained devices is feasible, and other participants agreed. Code size and performance depend on the chosen feature set: more features mean a more complex result, and the engineer must decide which features matter for a deployment and what trade-offs are acceptable.

The three common constraints are code size, energy consumption and bandwidth, and a design that optimizes all three at once is hard to find. Lowering memory use, for example, can raise communication overhead. The participants repeated the message from the earlier workshop: gains from Moore's law in the embedded space tend to go into lower cost and power rather than into more computing power, so designers will keep working under these constraints. Omitting security is not an option, but fitting it must not water down its effectiveness.

Two findings stand out. Execution time for expensive operations such as asymmetric signature generation and verification was within acceptable limits even on very constrained devices, and public key cryptography will likely be used only for the initial setup of symmetric session keys. Perhaps surprisingly, the energy cost of sending data wirelessly dwarfs expensive computations, and wireless reception is the most power-consuming task, so protocols must be designed with that in mind. The biggest savings come from optimizing the whole protocol stack, not just the cryptographic algorithms, and the participants noted that scalability of a security protocol does not imply usability.
sections.plainLanguage: Small devices can run real security protocols, and the hard part is choosing which features to keep. Sending data over the air uses more energy than the heavy calculations do, so the whole system has to be designed together rather than optimized in one place.

sections.title: Authorization and Access Control
sections.content:
Authorization is the approval granted to a system entity to use a system resource. Deciding it requires a view of the whole smart object lifecycle: when and how a device was added, what permissions it has, and how users may interact with it. The RFC names two broad schemes: systems that match an authenticated identifier against an access control list, and trait-based mechanisms that separate identity from rights and use roles and other attributes to grant or deny access.

Richard Barnes argued that the model that dominates the web today will not be enough for smart objects, because it binds all capabilities to credentials, and that access control is moving toward granting third parties specific capabilities. OAuth is given as an example of that direction. At the time of the workshop OAuth was focused on HTTP-based protocols, with early work to integrate it with the Simple Authentication and Security Layer and the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface, and its suitability for smart objects still needed investigation.

Other talks looked at where authorization decisions are made. In an Authentication, Authorization and Accounting context the decision happens at the server after the user is authenticated and is enforced by the client for the life of the session; the dynamic authorization extension to RADIUS also lets the server change or end a session already granted. The RFC notes that devices limited in code size, storage and connectivity may not suit established schemes, since delegating every decision costs network overhead while storing complex policies on the device may not fit. It is not clear whether new authorization mechanisms are needed; Kerberos, OAuth, EAP/AAA and attribute certificates already carry authorization, and in many cases the decisions are internal to the system and need no new standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication proves who a device is, while authorization decides what it may do. There is no single right method: some systems check a list, others use roles or grants, and existing tools already cover many cases.

sections.title: Provisioning Credentials
sections.content:
Before a smart object can be used it usually has to be given credentials: some identifier, keying material and other configuration such as the servers it must talk to. Some devices arrive pre-configured with default codes or passwords, or with per-device or per-user credentials. The available solutions depend on the interfaces the device has, and they differ between the enterprise and the consumer household. In large deployments the time needed to pair two objects rules out schemes that rely on manual steps.

Johannes Gilger discussed pairing and imprinting, which establish a security association between two equal devices such as Bluetooth phones. To resist man-in-the-middle attacks during that phase, devices with a display can show a number on each device for the user to compare, and devices with a keypad can require a PIN. Pairing is not necessarily a one-time event, which raises the question of group pairing or reducing it to pairwise pairing with a central master device. Cullen Jennings presented a model based on IP phones in which the device phones home to a manufacturer's server when first switched on, and that first contact is used to manage the device and give it keying material. Proof of ownership could be by identifying the purchaser, or by a secret enclosed in the packaging.

The participants worried about dependence on the manufacturer. A compromise of the manufacturer must not affect devices already imprinted to their owners, and questions arise when a manufacturer goes bankrupt, changes scope or is bought, or when a device is resold and ownership must be transferred. Industrial users accept relying on the manufacturer during imprinting but want exclusive control afterwards. Some devices must be imprinted completely offline, and the RFC asks how a device should behave if it is connected but never enrolled. The safest option for the user is to withhold full functionality until it has been enrolled, a concern sharpened by devices sold with default passwords.
sections.plainLanguage: A new device must be given secret keys before it can talk safely, sometimes at the factory, sometimes by the owner, and sometimes by contacting the maker. The hard questions are what happens if the maker disappears or is compromised, and how ownership passes when a device is sold.

sections.title: Summary and Follow-Up
sections.content:
The RFC's summary frames the whole exercise as an optimization decision that weighs technical aspects, usage scenarios, security threats and business models. Some constraints are fixed and some are flexible, and compromises are unavoidable, but they should not be made at the expense of security. Building in a software update mechanism is crucial so that features can be added and vulnerabilities fixed, and because threats are perceived differently over time; the RFC notes that many people considered pervasive monitoring less important before the Snowden revelations.

The participants did not think new research and standardization on cryptographic algorithms tailored to smart objects was worthwhile. A huge range of algorithms already exists, and standardized authentication and key exchange protocols can be customized to use almost any of them. Integrating the available building blocks into a working system was seen as the real problem, and searching for a single universal smart object security architecture was called a hopeless journey given the number of use cases, business models and constraints.

Follow-up work did happen. The Light-Weight Implementation Guidance working group was created to collect experience from implementers of IP stacks, including security protocols, on constrained devices; the DTLS In Constrained Environments working group was formed to define a DTLS profile suitable for Internet of Things applications and to describe how the DTLS record layer can carry multicast messages securely; and a new group, Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments, had just started to standardize authentication and authorization with fine-grained access control using a trusted third party.
sections.plainLanguage: The workshop judged smart object security as a set of trade-offs, not a single design, and saw software updates as essential. Rather than invent new cryptography, it pointed to reusing existing protocols, and several IETF groups were created to carry the work forward.

viz.caption: THE THREE COMMON CONSTRAINTS NAMED IN THE RFC

items.title: Code size
items.text: Room for the security protocol in the device's software, which more features make larger.

items.title: Energy consumption
items.text: Wireless reception is the most power-consuming task, and sending data costs more energy than heavy computation.

items.title: Bandwidth
items.text: The amount of data the link can carry, which security messaging adds to.
